papers.summary: Practitioners building training corpora with a pipeline of language models keep a preprocessing or refinement (post-process) stage when switching it on raises the corpus quality. We ablate a production pipeline that turns conference speech into question-answer pairs. The preprocessing stage rewrites the transcript, and the refinement stage filters the generated pairs. Switching each on and off gives four corpora from the same 40 Korean medical and finance sessions. On the corpus itself, quality rises as the stages switch on. Four LLM judges and six human domain experts rank the four corpora the same way, and the fully refined corpus leads by +0.18 and +0.22 on a 1-5 scale. We then ask whether that gain carries downstream. We supply each corpus to six models at inference and measure retrieval accuracy. The ranking does not hold. Enabling the transcript rewrite lowers retrieval accuracy by 0.061, the only stage effect that survives correction for multiple comparisons. That stage also reads the whole session, so it almost doubles the cost of one. With both stages on, accuracy does not change. An equivalence test we declared in advance confirms this. The corpus itself is clearly valuable. It lifts retrieval accuracy from 0.231 to 0.748 in every model and domain we test. More than a third of its pairs carry knowledge that neither of two frontier models produces on its own. On our data, the null does not come from weak corpora. A rising score on a rubric of this kind did not predict what the corpus holds for a model.

papers.title: A Two-Way Street: Surveying the Interplay between Code-Mixing and Native Languages in Text and Speech
papers.summary: Systems for code-mixed (CM) text and speech rarely start from scratch. CM data is scarce, so most work borrows from the languages being mixed, which we call native languages. This transfer can also run in reverse, when CM data is used to improve models for the native languages. Existing surveys focus on processing CM itself, and none brings the two directions together. This paper fills that gap with a systematic survey of transfer in both directions, across text and speech. We organise the surveyed work in a taxonomy of transfer direction, route and modality. Through this taxonomy, we find that most transfer runs from native languages into the CM setting. The reverse direction is younger, and in it code-switching mainly helps by aligning the two languages. Text and speech work share methods but rarely cite each other. On a shared speech benchmark, native data helps more than new architectures. These findings point to open challenges, such as how much native and CM data to mix in training, and how to evaluate CM text written in different scripts.

papers.title: When Does Hate Transfer? A Large-Scale Study of Cross-Lingual Hate Speech Detection
papers.summary: Effective detection of hate content is essential for maintaining healthy online communities, yet performance can vary substantially across languages. This work investigates a core practical question: Can training data from one language support hate-speech detection in another language with comparable performance? To answer this question, we conduct a large-scale study across 14 languages. \change{We observe consistent patterns in which certain language pairs transfer more effectively than others. Among the factors we measure, linguistic similarity is the strongest predictor of these patterns, with temporal overlap and dataset-size difference playing smaller roles. These measurable factors do not fully explain the observed patterns; a complementary qualitative analysis suggests that shared cultural cues and communicative norms may be associated with some of the remaining cases, particularly within several clusters. We present this cultural interpretation as a hypothesis from qualitative inspection rather than a measured cause.}{} Our analysis includes low-resource languages, offering practical insights into when cross-lingual transfer can support them and where its limitations emerge. These findings inform the design of more reliable multilingual hate-detection systems.

papers.title: Beyond Omni: A Unified MLLM for Embodied Sensory Understanding
papers.summary: Recent embodied systems increasingly build on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for their pretrained understanding and reasoning capabilities, but their perception of the physical world remains largely limited to basic modalities such as vision and audio. However, broadening MLLMs to more diverse sensory modalities from the physical environment is challenging: their representations are often weakly connected to the MLLM and vary substantially in structure and statistics, while their interpretation still requires shared high-level understanding and reasoning. We therefore propose Unisense, a unified embodied MLLM framework that supports diverse physical sensory modalities within a shared multimodal architecture. Unisense follows a two-stage training process: (i) aligning sensory representations with language to establish a language-accessible interface; and (ii) tuning modality-specific experts within the shared LLM to provide specialized processing for different sensory modalities. To support broad sensory learning, we curate Unisense-1M, a large-scale embodied sensory training corpus comprising 1M samples across 8 sensory modalities. We further evaluate Unisense on 12 benchmarks spanning depth, point cloud, IMU, tactile, thermal, radar, motion, and smell understanding. Across these heterogeneous sensing tasks, Unisense achieves strong performance and outperforms both generalist and specialized models on most benchmarks, demonstrating the potential of pretrained MLLMs as unified models for embodied sensory understanding.

papers.title: Honeyed Words, Hidden Daggers: Benchmarking and Training LLMs to See Through Mock Politeness
papers.summary: The Chinese idiom "kou mi fu jian" ("honeyed words, hidden daggers") names speech that is polite in form but hostile in function. We present ZhenhuanBench, a 1,592-item benchmark built from expert commentary on Empresses in the Palace, covering speaker intent, emotion-language mismatch, and per-listener uptake. Text-only evaluation covers 34 LLMs. GPT-6 Astra leads the leaderboard at 73.48% overall, while its listener-reaction score is 58.37%. The annotations also supply supervised traces and string-verifiable training rewards. With 338 gold traces, an 8B model outperforms teacher distillation on identical items. Subsequent RL saturates, and chance correction reduces the estimated recoverable performance gap by a factor of 7.5. Our CPR-GRPO loop (Compress-Probe-Replenish) uses this estimate to weight gold supervision, reaching 67.0 on public multiple-choice tasks and 74.5 under the training-matched hidden protocol. Without target-task training, CPR outperforms Base, SFT, and GRPO across six Chinese and English pragmatic and sarcasm evaluations. On three external datasets, training with CPR yields higher mean Macro-F1 than SFT and GRPO.

papers.title: Assertion and Belief: Moore's Paradox in Language Models
papers.summary: Moore's paradox \citep{moore1942} concerns sentences such as ``It is raining, but I don't believe that it is,'' which may well be true yet cannot be sensibly asserted. The absurdity lies not in the content but in the act, since to assert is to vouch for one's own belief. This makes the paradox a test of whether language models take the speech act into account when computing meaning. We present the first test of Moore's paradox in LLMs, evaluating 12 models on a curated set of Moorean sentences in varied contexts. We find that models largely recognize the infelicity of Moorean sentences, and that the judgement is not tied to a memorized form and tracks the speech act. Using the Rational Speech Act framework (RSA; \citealt{goodmanfrank2016}), we then test whether these judgements arise from a listener reasoning about a speaker. We find the models' own listeners do not reason about their own speakers, and their reasoning traces suggest that they instead recall knowledge about the paradox and apply rules therein. The models thus appear to have learned the paradox as a fact about sentences, not as a requirement on speakers.

papers.title: Local Evidence, Global Failure: Diagnosing Speech-Vision Temporal Composition in Audio-Visual Language Models
papers.summary: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) can fail at full-video speech-vision decisions even when useful visual evidence is locally recoverable. We introduce Temporal Evidence Decomposition (TED), a training-free diagnostic framework that separates local visual verification from speech-relative aggregation. Automatic speech recognition supplies a transcript and utterance interval. TED queries audio-free windows with the transcript for Temporal Alignment and Forecasting, or answer candidates for Cross-Modal Temporal Binding, then aggregates evidence relative to that interval. Across four frozen AV-LLMs on SVHalluc, Temporal Forecasting accuracy rises from 29.3-33.7% under full-video questioning to 79.3-82.2% with TED. Query replacement reduces recovery; the observed anchor remains beneficial when temporal-region availability is held fixed. Physical-isolation and timing-shortcut controls test alternative explanations. The findings distinguish locally recoverable evidence from successful full-video decisions, motivating explicit separation of narration content, utterance timing, and time-indexed visual evidence.

papers.title: Beyond the Benchmark: Conditioning, Domains and Failure Modes of Qwen3-TTS
papers.summary: Qwen3-TTS reports state-of-the-art zero-shot voice cloning, but its technical report leaves open how the model should be conditioned, how it behaves outside read speech, and how it fails. We characterise its two cloning interfaces, in-context learning (ICL) and X-Vector, against Chatterbox, XTTS-v2 and F5-TTS on read, meeting, emotional and air-traffic-control (ATC) speech, using eighteen objective measures, an LLM judge, a spoofing countermeasure and a listening test. Neither interface dominates: ICL clones timbre more closely from correctly transcribed references, X-Vector clones timing, and ICL degrades sharply when a short reference transcript is wrong. Domain explains four times more variance than system choice. Qwen3-TTS leads on intelligibility and pitch register but trails on prosody, and the objective measures rank systems differently from listeners. An off-the-shelf countermeasure flags its clones no more often than genuine recordings, and on ATC radio it fails for every system. Code and audio are released.

papers.title: Do Speech BCIs Need Larger Models? Rethinking Neural Decoding beyond Scaling
papers.summary: Recent speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) increasingly rely on large models and complex multi-stage pipelines for neural decoding. However, in speech BCI, where training data are scarce, noisy, and expensive to collect, the benefits of model scaling remain unclear. This work revisits a fundamental question: are large models truly necessary for accurate neural decoding? We propose BEST (Brain-Encoding-Speech-Text), a two-stage framework for efficient neural-to-text decoding. Instead of relying on large generative models or phoneme-centric pipelines, BEST introduces hierarchical intermediate representations and a compact speech-oriented decoder that directly maps neural activity to text. This design preserves essential structure while significantly reducing computational cost, enabling robust generalization in low-resource settings and practical deployment under constrained resources. On the Brain-to-Text '24 and '25 benchmarks, BEST achieves word error rates (WERs) of 6.19% and 1.62%, respectively, using only 3.85% of the parameters required by comparable methods. Beyond these results, we provide three key insights: (1) decoder scaling yields non-monotonic gains; (2) cross-modal alignment is more critical than model size; and (3) overfitting degards sequence-level performance. Representation analysis further reveals a consistent neural-audio-text alignment pathway.

papers.title: MUB: An Identity-Masked Benchmark for Music Understanding in Multimodal Language Models
papers.summary: Evaluating musical perception in multimodal language models requires separating audio evidence from answers recoverable through metadata or external tools. We present the Music Understanding Benchmark (MUB), a locally assembled collection of 500 identity-masked recordings with existing annotations for tempo, key, time signature, and structural intervals. The collection covers all 24 major/minor key combinations, tempos of 47--180 beats per minute, and 4,676 annotated intervals. Original titles, artists, and platform identifiers are excluded from evaluation inputs. Relative to recent music question-answering and temporal-grounding work, MUB emphasizes scalar tempo prediction and full-recording interval outputs, together with a documented metadata-masking protocol. Saved baseline predictions yield 53.6\% tempo accuracy for a simple DSP estimator and 98.4\% time-signature accuracy for a constant 4/4 predictor. We identify important limitations, including an asymmetric legacy key metric, unverified independent annotation agreement, extreme metre imbalance, and unresolved recording-level rights clearance. No contemporary multimodal language model comparison has yet been completed. MUB is therefore an evaluation resource and protocol under validation, rather than a completed demonstration of model capabilities.

papers.title: Too Emotional to Be Fake? Intra-Utterance Emotion Shifts Expose Failure Modes in Speech Deepfake Detectors
papers.summary: Expressive speech synthesis can now change emotion within a single utterance, yet its impact on deepfake detection remains unclear. We introduce EmoShift, a benchmark comparing emotion-stable (AA) and emotion-changing (AB) speech to examine these effects while accounting for static emotion identity and acoustic confounds. It comprises 7,240 bona fide utterances from four source datasets and 9,720 synthetic utterances generated using four expressive TTS systems. Across seven detectors, we find that emotion changes can make synthetic speech appear more genuine, increasing spoof miss rates by up to 25.3 percentage points on OMG-Emotion at fixed thresholds. Conversely, emotion-changing bona fide speech increases false-alarm rates by up to 24.4 percentage points on IEMOCAP. Further analyses reveal detector-specific sensitivities to emotion trajectories, not fully explained by static emotion identity or splicing artifacts. These findings underscore the importance of emotion dynamics in deepfake detection.

papers.title: Rethinking Batch Composition: Promoting Feature Diversity for Speech Enhancement
papers.summary: Speech enhancement systems are commonly trained using randomly sampled mini-batches, which may contain limited diversity in intrinsic acoustic characteristics of the clean speech signals. Motivated by previous findings linking clean speech characteristics to enhancement performance, we propose a feature-stratified mini-batch sampling strategy that divides training examples into quantiles according to a clean-speech characteristic and enforces equal representation within each mini-batch. Experiments across two large-scale English and Spanish speech datasets and a smaller dataset containing neurotypical and pathological speech demonstrate improvements over standard random mini-batch sampling across multiple objective enhancement metrics. Ablation studies demonstrate that the gains are robust across training runs, while their magnitude depends on the acoustic characteristic used for stratification. The proposed strategy requires no modification to the enhancement model or training objective, providing a simple and complementary approach to speech enhancement training.

papers.title: A hidden Markov model for unsupervised EEG-based tracking of auditory attention to a single voice
papers.summary: Objective: Absolute auditory attention decoding (aAAD) aims to track how strongly a listener attends to a single speech source using electroencephalography (EEG). Unlike selective auditory attention decoding, aAAD lacks a competing speech reference, making reliable attention tracking challenging. Approach: We propose a fully unsupervised aAAD pipeline combining neural envelope tracking (NET) with hidden Markov model (HMM)-based temporal inference. Using EEG signals and the target speech envelope, the framework estimates a continuous attention trajectory without explicit attention-state labels. We evaluate the approach using EEG recordings from 30 adults, investigate the impact of analysis window length, and compare HMM post-processing with moving-average (MA) smoothing and alternative EEG features. Main results: With 1-s analysis windows, non-causal HMM post-processing improves the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for all 30 participants, increasing mean AUC from 0.547 for raw NET to 0.832. A 5-s window achieves the highest mean AUC of 0.858. Compared with non-causal MA smoothing, the HMM achieves higher AUC across the examined smoothing scales. Individual switch detection times are comparable, while the HMM generally achieves lower group-level detection times. NET also outperforms alpha power and spectral entropy as an observation feature in the unsupervised HMM framework. Significance: The proposed framework provides a label-free approach for estimating temporal fluctuations in auditory attention, demonstrating the utility of probabilistic temporal inference for continuous attention tracking in single-speaker listening scenarios.

papers.title: When Does "Post-Call" Begin? An Availability Contract for Earnings-Call NLP Benchmarks
papers.summary: Corporate financial disclosures often unfold over time, with announcements, prepared remarks, and discussion spanning multiple high-frequency return intervals. Financial NLP benchmarks can therefore suffer from a within-event timing mismatch when the prediction target begins before the textual or audio input used by a model could be complete. Chronological train--test splits do not prevent this mismatch, because it occurs inside individual events rather than across samples. We introduce an Availability Contract, which requires a benchmark to state the input boundary, evidence for input availability, the outcome start, and the claims supported by that evidence. We apply this framework to 552 earnings calls from 24 firms. For each call, we hold the return endpoint fixed and compare the previous close, a documentary call-start proxy, and a completion proxy based on reconstructed audio end plus a stipulated processing allowance. At this baseline, moving from the call-start proxy to the completion proxy flips return signs for 9.4% of calls. Holding completion-clock cutpoints fixed, 28.3% change quintile. In an independent release-session analysis of a public earnings-call volatility benchmark, shifting before-market target windows forward by one trading session raises three-day mean squared error by 18.1-21.4% across four frozen prediction streams, while their point rankings remain unchanged. Together, the results show that labels and losses can depend materially on the declared outcome clock even when model rankings appear stable. The Availability Contract makes this assumption explicit and ties post-input claims to the available timing evidence.

papers.title: Hear, Localize, and Reason: Spatially Aware Scene Understanding for Audio-Visual LLMs
papers.summary: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) have made strong progress in multimodal understanding, yet most treat audio as monaural semantic content, limiting their ability to reason about where sounds originate and how they relate to the visual scene. Recent spatial audio-visual studies address parts of this problem, but often focus on specific abilities, such as spatial correspondence or direction and distance reasoning. In this work, we introduce HLR-AVSceneQA, a comprehensive benchmark with a hear-localize-reason hierarchy that evaluates whether models can recognize what is heard, localize sound sources in egocentric and allocentric views, and use these localized sources to reason about how they relate to the visual scene. We further introduce HLR-LLM, which augments a strong audio-visual foundation model with a binaural spatial audio branch alongside its monaural semantic audio pathway. We train HLR-LLM with a curriculum that incorporates final-stage chain-of-thought supervision for multi-step spatial reasoning. Experiments show that existing AV-LLMs remain limited in spatial grounding and relational reasoning, while HLR-LLM substantially improves spatial audio-visual scene understanding without compromising semantic audio-visual perception.

papers.title: How large an effect would we have seen? Positive controls, detection floors and dataset pitfalls in scalp-EEG speech decoding
papers.summary: Objective. Studies that decode imagined speech from scalp electroencephalography (EEG) commonly validate their pipelines with a positive control, usually overt speech, and report null results without stating what effect size the pipeline could have detected. Approach. Using ds003626 ("Thinking out loud"), KaraOne and Track 3 of the 2020 International Brain-Computer Interface Competition, we audited decoding of overt speech, articulator preparation and imagined speech with artifact-channel subsets, band-limited decoding and trial selection, under a protocol that enforces split integrity by assertion. We injected class-dependent effects of known amplitude into the real recordings to measure the detection floor of five decoder families, and we checked the ds003626 labels against the dataset's acquisition protocol. Main results. On ds003626, two lip electrodes decoded overt speech at 0.7430 and the eight external channels at 0.7068, against 0.4231 for the 128-channel scalp montage, and no decodable signal survived in the 8-30 Hz band. On the other two corpora, within-subject accuracy rose monotonically with frequency into the range dominated by muscle activity. Band-power logistic regression detected an injected 8-30 Hz desynchronization of 0.54 uV under a criterion fixed in advance, whereas a compact convolutional network (EEGNet) detected nothing within subject up to 4.31 uV. In ds003626, the condition codes are the reverse of the intuitive reading, the class encoding changed between public releases, and condition is a deterministic function of time within each session. Significance. In these corpora the overt-speech positive control is dominated by myogenic signal and cannot validate a decoding pipeline. We recommend that speech-decoding studies report band-limited and artifact-channel accuracy, the direction of accuracy across frequency, and a measured detection floor.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Spoken Language Understanding with SLAM-ASR: What Do Monolingual ASR-Trained Linear Projectors Enable?
papers.summary: The SLAM-ASR framework connects the features of a frozen speech encoder as input to a frozen LLM decoder to enable speech transcription. In this work we ask whether this training-on speech transcription-provides the LLM with the capability to also perform spoken language understanding (SLU) tasks, by training monolingual projectors on 11 languages. When prompted to answer a yes/no question about the input speech, the mean instruction following rate (IFR) is 49.8%. When not following the instruction, these models default back to transcription. The transcription quality-measured by the character error rate (CER)-is not sufficient to predict IFR. Remarkably, when the model is instructed to answer the topic question as a single digit option, the mean IFR rises to 81.3%. Our models score a mean 23.2% topic balanced accuracy (BAcc) against 14.3% chance. However, the same decoder scores a mean 71.5% BAcc when using reference transcripts as text input. This indicates a failure of the projector to transfer information for the SLU tasks.

papers.title: What Does LALM Post-training Learn? Rethinking Audio Understanding and Reasoning Capabilities
papers.summary: Post-training often improves the performance of large audio-language models on audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks. However, these improvements may reflect adaptation to specific question formats, such as multiple-choice questions, rather than genuine advances in audio understanding and reasoning capabilities. To investigate what LALMs actually learn from post-training, we conduct controlled experiments that disentangle improvements in audio understanding from adaptation to specific question formats. Across different models and post-training methods, we find that much of the reported improvement persists even without informative audio, but largely disappears when the question format changes. These findings suggest that post-training often teaches models to exploit task-specific textual cues and answer patterns rather than developing generalizable audio understanding and reasoning capabilities.

papers.title: OmniCompass: A Holistic Benchmark for Omni-Modal Video Grounding and Understanding
papers.summary: With the rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), evaluating their video understanding capabilities has become increasingly important. Existing video understanding benchmarks cover only part of the evaluation dimensions, limiting systematic diagnosis of omni-modal video understanding. We introduce OmniCompass, a holistic benchmark for omni-modal video grounding and understanding. OmniCompass defines two evaluation tracks: OmniCompass-VL assesses vision-language models on tasks requiring visual evidence, while OmniCompass-AV assesses omni-modal models on tasks requiring joint audio-visual evidence. Each track includes three complementary tasks: temporal grounding (TG), spatial grounding (SG), and question answering (QA), assessing when a referenced target appears, where it is, and what happens. QA covers five perception and three reasoning categories in OmniCompass-VL, and three perception and two reasoning categories in OmniCompass-AV. OmniCompass-VL contains 820 videos and 2,460 instances across domains and three duration types: short, medium, and long. A narrative- and audio-rich subset forms OmniCompass-AV with 240 videos and 720 instances. Each instance is evaluated under two paired settings: text-only and text+image, specifying the same target through text and visual-language guidance. All instances are manually annotated with multi-round quality verification. Evaluations of 50 MLLMs show that open-source models still lag behind proprietary counterparts, particularly in audio-visual understanding. Precise temporal and spatial grounding remains challenging even for leading models, and their predictions still exhibit inconsistencies across the paired target specifications.

papers.title: PhonoVoxtLM: Exploring Single-Codebook Phonological Tokens for Speech Understanding and Generation
papers.summary: We investigate how speech token representations can support both understanding and generation within a unified speech language model. We present PhonoVoxtLM, built on the existing VoxtLM framework using phonological tokens designed to retain linguistic content and prosodic information. The existing tokenizer is jointly trained for speech recognition and resynthesis. Its single-codebook units serve as both speech inputs and generation targets, without additional speech-token prediction modules. Experiments show improvements over HuBERT-based baselines across understanding and generation under different training-data scales. Further comparisons with WavLM-based tokens reveal trade-offs between recognition and synthesis, highlighting the importance of evaluating shared representations across both capabilities. We further extend the framework to spoken question answering through fine-tuning with replay. The adapted model improves answering performance over similarly adapted HuBERT baselines while retaining advantages on the original speech tasks. Our findings support single-codebook representations designed for both content and prosody as a practical choice for unified multitask speech modeling.

papers.title: Estimating Surprisal from the Speech Signal
papers.summary: Although language is predominantly spoken, empirical tests of surprisal theory rely almost entirely on written text. In practice, surprisal is estimated using language models (LMs) trained on text and applied to transcriptions, creating a text bottleneck that limits evaluation of the theory in the spoken modality. We remove this bottleneck by estimating surprisal directly from the speech signal using a speech LM. This raises a key question: should surprisal be defined over realization-specific acoustic inputs or over abstract linguistic units? Since a single unit can have many distinct acoustic realizations, each assigned a different probability by the model, defining surprisal over abstract units is difficult. To address this, we introduce an importance sampling estimator that approximates the probability of an abstract unit by marginalizing over realizations generated by a text-to-speech model. Using pupillometry data from a listening study, we evaluate surprisal theory in this text-free setting at multiple levels of granularity. Obtaining surprisal from several speech LMs, we consistently find that surprisal estimated via importance sampling better predicts pupil dilation than realization-specific surprisal for words. We also find that surprisal values for sub-lexical units are predictive of pupil dilation. While we find that surprisal can be estimated without recourse to text, and that marginalizing over distinct realizations of words is more predictive of lexical processing effort, surprisal as a whole is not a strong predictor of change in pupil size, regardless of its source.

papers.title: DualAffect: Dual-Path Paralinguistic Integration for Generative Audiovisual Emotion Understanding
papers.summary: Understanding human emotion is essential for multimodal systems that interpret both the content of an interaction and the speaker's expressive state. However, connecting paralinguistic cues to generated answers remains challenging, particularly when vocal expression diverges from visual appearance. We propose DualAffect, a dual-path architecture that integrates visually conditioned acoustic features and temporally organized acoustic tokens into a shared language decoder. The two pathways reuse the same acoustic encoding. The fusion pathway associates sound with visual content through visual queries, while the direct pathway compresses the valid acoustic sequence into ordered tokens through an independent projector. This design gives the decoder access to both joint audiovisual context and acoustic evidence organized along its own timeline. Mixed-task adaptation with task-dependent output preservation supports emotion recognition and general audiovisual question answering within the same model. DualAffect achieves an average metric of 67.89 on CA-MER and accuracies of 62.88% on the EmotionTalk test set and 49.87% on Daily-Omni. Pathway interventions show that the trained decoder uses direct acoustic evidence alongside existing fusion. With model parameters and fusion inputs fixed, zeroing the direct tokens reduces EmotionTalk validation accuracy by 9.75 percentage points and the CA-MER average metric by 2.66 points. The largest CA-MER subset effect occurs when the overall emotion agrees with audio but differs from vision. These findings identify acoustic representation organization as a practical design axis for connecting paralinguistic perception to unified audiovisual generation. Code is available at https://github.com/YiboWang2002/DualAffect.

papers.title: Understanding Machine Taste: Aesthetic Agreement Across Foundation Models in K-pop
papers.summary: As foundation models enter creative industries, understanding their aesthetic preferences becomes an important step toward AI-assisted creative decision making. In this work, we investigate how foundation models evaluate creative content and characterize their ``machine taste'' using K-pop songs and music videos as a testbed. We formulate aesthetic evaluation as a pairwise ranking problem and systematically examine pairwise inter-model agreement, group-level consensus, and cross-modal preference alignment. Our results reveal stronger pairwise inter-model agreement and group-level consensus in visual evaluation than in audio evaluation, while preferences across the two modalities remain weakly aligned. We further examine how visual consensus rankings relate to real-world popularity using historical YouTube viewership data, finding positive but varying correlations across artist groups. These findings provide initial insights into machine aesthetic preferences and lay the groundwork for future AI-assisted creative decision making that considers creative content, artist identity, audience preferences, and market dynamics.

papers.title: Safety for Whom? Benchmarking Understanding Beyond Refusal in Egocentric Multimodal Assistants
papers.summary: Egocentric multimodal assistants see through the user's eyes and guide what the user does next, so their outputs directly shape physical actions, including those that affect bystanders. Yet existing safety evaluations do not distinguish whom a response would harm, and score only whether a model refuses. Pooling all harms into one refusal rate hides two failures: a model may protect one target but not another, and it may refuse without understanding the risk, or understand it and comply anyway. We present STOU, a benchmark of 2,902 egocentric video-audio and video-text queries whose potential harm targets the user (Self), co-present individuals (The Others), or society at large (Others). Our evaluation decouples safety understanding from refusal behavior: beyond refusal, we score whether the model recognizes the user's intent, the presence and target of harm, and its downstream consequences. Across 10 open and closed source omnimodal and multimodal LLMs, we find that refusal varies systematically with the harm target, and that models often recognize a harm yet still assist with it. These results show that refusal rates alone cannot certify an assistant as safe, and that safety alignment must account for who would be harmed. Project page: https://onedayoneyeah.github.io/safety-for-whom

papers.title: ATTEST: Evidence-Grounded Reinforcement Learning for Long-Audio Temporal Understanding
papers.summary: Temporal grounding is fundamental to audio understanding, yet large audio language models (LALMs) remain weak at it on long audio, where hallucinations compound and annotated data is scarce. Existing benchmarks cover only short clips or offer coarse, synthetic annotations. We introduce EgoSCAPE, a manually verified benchmark created from Ego4D with 700 real audios of durations up to 5 minutes, annotated with dense captions, sound sources, audio timelines, and temporal grounding queries. We further propose ATTEST, a GRPO-based reinforcement learning framework that improves temporal grounding without changing the base model's architecture or token vocabulary. ATTEST combines (i) a counterfactual grounding reward penalizing predictions that survive removal of their acoustic evidence, (ii) an attention-density reward encouraging generation to attend to its own claimed time spans, and (iii) token-wise advantages giving segment-level credit for long dense captions. ATTEST outperforms prior temporal grounding methods on existing dense captioning and grounding benchmarks, with fewer hallucinations. Together, EgoSCAPE and ATTEST establish a rigorous evaluation-training recipe that brings temporally grounded audio understanding closer to practical, long-form deployment.

papers.title: The NVVSpeech Challenge 2026: Overview and Lessons for Speech Understanding and Generation with Nonverbal Vocalizations
papers.summary: Nonverbal vocalizations (NVVs), such as laughter and sighs, convey meaning alongside words. NVV-aware speech systems must recognize and generate these events while preserving lexical accuracy and perceptual quality. Yet differences in annotation, resources, and evaluation complicate comparisons, and aggregate scores can obscure specific weaknesses. We review ten system descriptions from the NVVSpeech Challenge 2026, covering understanding and generation in Chinese and English across 16 event categories. Our analysis examines supervision construction, task adaptation, and inference-time or preference-based feedback. Results reveal persistent recognition difficulties with breath and gasp and trade-offs between event recognition and lexical accuracy, as well as between generation intelligibility and acoustic quality, with human listening providing complementary evaluation evidence. These findings identify priorities for advancing NVV-aware speech understanding, controllable generation, and comparable evaluation.

papers.title: HMU-Bench: Hierarchical Music Understanding Benchmark for Omni Models
papers.summary: Music-understanding benchmarks should identify both the evidence available to a model and the operations a correct answer requires. We introduce HMU-Bench, a bilingual benchmark with notation and audio components. ABC Q&A contains 1,029 Chinese-English question pairs across six musical domains, labeled as extraction, single-step inference, or multi-step inference. Audio Q&A contains 460 question pairs on 92 recordings, spanning five scope-difficulty configurations. All music is Suno-generated, and questions and references are human-reviewed. Reference-based evaluation of seven omni models yields high notation scores for the strongest systems, but no model averages above 1.4 on the 0-4 audio scale. Notation and audio rankings show little correlation. A transposition case study also reveals octave errors missed by LLM grading. These findings motivate separate modality reporting and event-level checks for symbolic outputs. Data, annotations, evaluator prompts, and graded responses will be released at https://github.com/stepaudiollm/hmu-bench.

papers.title: From Acoustic Sensing to Physical Actions: A Comprehensive Survey of Security Risks in Edge-Deployed Audio LLM-Based Agents
papers.summary: Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) are embedded in agents for smart homes, vehicles, wearables, and embodied systems, where acoustic inputs can propagate from perception into persistent state and consequential execution. This setting extends security analysis beyond model behavior to the system conditions that determine how acoustic inputs can influence agent behavior and external actions. Existing surveys examine acoustic security, LLM-based agents, and edge deployment in isolation, leaving their security interactions in deployed Audio LLM-based agents insufficiently characterized. This survey introduces an Acoustic Sensing-to-Action (S2A) system model that traces these security implications along the path from acoustic sensing to external execution, while accounting for edge-cloud runtime and lifecycle transformation. We use the model to synthesize attacks, defenses, and evaluation methods across the acoustic, agent, and edge-system literature. The synthesis shows that security gaps can emerge within components and at the transitions between stages, where protections developed for one stage do not necessarily provide end-to-end assurance in the deployed system. These findings motivate security evaluation that follows acoustic influence from sensing to action across persistent state, system boundaries, and changing deployment conditions in real-world agents.

papers.title: "Is Low Power Enough?" Rethinking Energy Efficiency in High-Fidelity Sensing
papers.summary: For two decades, long-lived sensor nodes have been built from the lowest-power parts, because their scalar readings take only milliseconds to acquire and send. Scientists now want higher fidelity data from the field, such as images and audio, and these observations break that rule: a low-power microcontroller stays awake for seconds to read, store, and transmit each one, so low power is no longer low energy. We argue that long-lived, high-fidelity nodes should instead be built around a more capable microcontroller, provided the whole board sleeps deeply. We revisit two principles from early sensor networks, "race to sleep" and "talk less", for high-fidelity data and on-device AI, and test them by comparing the STM32N6, which pairs a fast core with a neural accelerator, against the low-power Apollo4 Plus. Although the STM32N6 draws 1.9x more power, it completes an observation (capture, storage, on-board detection, and a LoRa transmission) 9.9x faster and so uses 5.2x less energy. On the same model, it runs inference with 3.2-11.4x less energy, and it fits models over 23 points more accurate. A high-fidelity node lives longest when it finishes quickly, sleeps deeply, and sends only what matters.

papers.title: OpenSVBench: Diagnosing Speaker Verification Generalization Across Deployment Scenarios
papers.summary: Speaker verification (SV) systems now achieve very low error rates on standard public protocols, but those results do not fully describe deployment generalization. VoxCeleb-style evaluations remain useful anchors for English in-the-wild media speech. Scenario-specific evaluations and challenges are also valuable. However, neither setting directly shows whether the same system remains reliable across diverse deployment scenarios. We introduce OpenSVBench, a public benchmark for cross-scenario SV evaluation. Its fixed public core contains 26 trial sets organized into 11 scenario groups, with 9.15M verification trials, frozen target/non-target keys, and metadata for scenario-wise reporting. Around this core, the online leaderboard acts as a diagnostic evaluation interface rather than only a ranked list. It accepts score packages from new systems, evaluates them with frozen keys and common scoring, and reports trial-set breakdowns, scenario-group metrics, macro EER/minDCF, model-wise profiles, and scenario-wise comparisons. We evaluate 18 public checkpoints spanning x-vector, ECAPA-TDNN, CAMPPlus, ResNet and ERes variants, ReDimNet2, SAM-ResNet, and pretrained Transformer speaker recipes. The results show clear cross-scenario gaps: systems with similar macro EER can have different scenario profiles, strong performance in one scenario does not guarantee strong performance in another, and same-scenario trial sets can still expose source and protocol gaps.

papers.title: Personalization Without Stereotyping: Do Speech LLMs Know When to Turn a Deaf Ear?
papers.summary: Recent speech LLMs can leverage rich paralinguistic cues, enabling more complex and personalized interactions. However, little work investigates how this sensitivity can lead to stereotyping, and existing evaluations largely measure demographic disparities without distinguishing beneficial personalization from stereotypical behavior. We introduce BASIS-Bench, a benchmark designed to disentangle these two aspects through three axes: (1) demographic robustness, measuring disparities in content-based tasks across speakers and demographic classification capabilities; (2) stereotypical bias, measuring whether perceived demographic cues trigger unprompted stereotypical behavior; and (3) personalization, measuring whether models can tailor responses to demographic characteristics when explicitly requested. We evaluate eight recent speech LLMs and find that, despite often recognizing demographic cues, most fail to translate them into appropriate personalization. Explicit demographic labels improve personalization but also amplify stereotypical associations already present in the textual backbones. These findings highlight the need to train speech LLMs not only to perceive demographic cues, but to learn when they should shape their responses.

papers.title: Input Representation, Not Model Size or Pretraining Scale, Shapes Speaker Verification Robustness to Temporal Degradation
papers.summary: Speech remains intelligible to listeners under heavy temporal degradation, but whether speaker identity survives is largely unexplored. We evaluate six automatic speaker verification (ASV) models, trained on temporally intact speech, and tested under three degradations that remove different combinations of temporal cues. The models form three pairs, one per architecture family (convolutional, transformer, conformer), each pairing a waveform-input with a mel filterbank-input model. All models degrade, but robustness tracks input representation rather than pretraining scale or model size. In all nine family-by-condition comparisons the filterbank-input model degrades less, with eight of nine 95% confidence intervals excluding zero, even when it is smaller or has less pretraining than its waveform counterpart. In the controlled convolutional pair, where the models differ only in input representation, the filterbank-input model's equal error rate rises from 1.1% to 17.1% under the heaviest tested degradation, against 2.9% to29.7% for its waveform counterpart.

papers.title: When History Helps and Hurts: Selective History Use across Multimodal Turns
papers.summary: Reliable multimodal interaction depends on selective use of conversational history: an earlier question may remain relevant while its previous answer is outdated, whereas a current request may depend on historical evidence despite conflicting new observations. Existing multi-turn evaluations rarely separate these history-use demands from underlying question difficulty. To address this gap, we introduce ReTurn, a benchmark of 7,000 base tasks spanning visual and audio evidence for evaluating selective history use. For task-carrying history, Reconfirm/Reground require applying a historical question to current media while varying historical agreement; for evidence-carrying history, Retrieve/Rebind require answering a current question using historical media while varying current-media competition. Each pair preserves the target question, media, and answer. Tasks support open-ended and multiple-choice evaluation, with matched single-turn counterparts serving as answerability references. Across 13 omni-modal, vision-language, and audio-language models, median model-level open-ended accuracy falls from 93.7% with direct input to 72.3% in conversation. Behavioral probes show that high question recall can coexist with weaker task application, while competing media can redirect answers away from historical targets. Supervised adaptation yields only partial gains. ReTurn provides a controlled framework for assessing whether multimodal models select and use the historical information required by each request.

papers.title: When Can You Prune Your Network? A Study of Intermediate Neurons in Multilingual Speech Parsing
papers.summary: End-to-end speech parsing, a task recently proposed, consists in predicting both the transcription and the syntactic tree for a spoken utterance. Existing architectures for speech parsing often utilise intermediate neural networks. In this work, we examine the effectiveness of intermediate neural networks (NN) for parsing, and, specifically, what role do they play. We introduce a simpler end-to-end architecture for speech parsing, where we remove these intermediate NN units, reducing the parameters by 12%, while achieving comparable or better performance than prior method on both automatic speech recognition (ASR) and parsing. We demonstrate that intermediate NN units help reduce the representational gap when the pre-trained encoder is frozen. We do a comprehensive evaluation of speech parsing on French, and medium-low resource languages Slovenian and Naija. We further investigate the impact of the training data size and intermediate layers of the pretrained speech encoder on speech parsing.

papers.title: MiDashengLM-Spatial: Unifying General Audio Understanding and Spatial Awareness
papers.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) have achieved strong performance in general audio understanding, yet most are designed for monaural input and discard the inter-channel cues essential for spatial perception. In contrast, existing spatial audio-language models are purpose-built for spatial tasks and fail to capitalize on the general understanding capabilities of monaural LALMs. We present MiDashengLM-Spatial, the first open-source end-to-end unified audio-language model, to our knowledge, which supports both general audio understanding and spatial awareness within a single architecture. It extends MiDashengLM with a spatial audio encoder, Spatial-Dasheng, integrated through a hierarchical semantic-to-spatial conditioning module that injects intermediate semantic representations into the spatial branch at multiple depths while preserving the original semantic pathway. To provide spatial audio-language supervision at scale, we develop a data synthesis pipeline that renders diverse spatial acoustic scenes with scene-level spatial descriptions and question-answer pairs. Experiments show that Spatial-Dasheng achieves strong performance on sound event localization and detection in real-world scenes, and that MiDashengLM-Spatial substantially outperforms existing LALMs on spatial understanding and reasoning benchmarks. Meanwhile, it remains competitive with state-of-the-art 8B-scale LALMs on diverse monaural benchmarks, demonstrating that spatial awareness can be acquired without compromising general audio understanding. The source code and model checkpoint are available at https://github.com/xiaomi-research/midashenglm-spatial and https://huggingface.co/mispeech/midashenglm-spatial.

papers.title: InterView-C: A Synchronized Multimodal Corpus of VR Avatar-Mediated Survey Interviews
papers.summary: We present InterView-C, a German multimodal corpus of 27 survey interviews conducted entirely in virtual reality, with both interlocutors represented by avatars. The corpus aligns spoken interaction with synchronized behavioral data, including gaze, head and body movement, facial behavior, hand and finger tracking. Its reference transcripts and linguistic annotations provide a reliable interface between this multimodal spoken interaction and predominantly text-based NLP methods. This interface is important because automatically transcribing speech can distort linguistically relevant information, while downstream models trained on existing resources may additionally face transfer challenges when applied to transcribed spoken data. InterView-C therefore provides word-timed and manually post-edited verbatim transcripts for all 54 recordings, interview-item timings, questionnaire responses and negation cue and scope annotations for 1,422 sentences, 1,398 of them doubly annotated (α=0.87 for cues; α=0.81 for scopes). We demonstrate both challenges empirically: nine open-weight ASR systems disproportionately misrecognize short closed answers and number words, while negation models trained on existing corpora show lower and highly variable performance on our transcribed interviews than a model trained on the InterView-C annotations. InterView-C thus enables linguistic analyses of spoken interaction while retaining their alignment with rich multimodal behavior.

papers.title: SAVU-BENCH: A Real-World Benchmark for Spatial Audio-Visual Understanding
papers.summary: Spatial audio-visual understanding requires models to recognize not only what is present, but also where events occur and how they relate across modalities. Existing benchmarks often rely on simulated scenes, evaluate isolated spatial skills, and provide limited diagnostic insight into failure modes. We introduce SAVU-Bench, a real-world benchmark that systematically evaluates spatial audio-visual understanding across three capability levels and seven evaluation tasks. We further introduce SAVU-Diag, a scene-linked diagnostic set that decomposes reasoning questions into their prerequisite grounding and alignment sub-tasks. Evaluation of 12 representative models on SAVU-Bench reveals that while visual spatial grounding is relatively mature, spatial perception involving audio remains a primary bottleneck. SAVU-Diag further demonstrates that most reasoning errors co-occur with failures on these prerequisite tasks, though reasoning gaps persist even when prerequisites are correctly resolved. Motivated by these findings, we introduce SAVU-EA, a training-free evidence-augmented baseline that makes spatial cues more explicit. While SAVU-EA substantially improves spatial grounding and joint matching, high-level spatial reasoning remains challenging. Our findings highlight the urgent need for both robust spatial audio perception and deeper integration of cross-modal spatial relations.

papers.title: EC-RAG: Event Chain Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Long Video Understanding
papers.summary: Current large video-language models (LVLMs) still face challenges when dealing with long videos, mainly because frames are often processed independently, making it difficult to capture temporal dependencies across events. Although retrieval-augmented approaches have been introduced to provide additional context, most of them operate at the frame or snippet level, which limits their ability to model how events evolve over time and relate to each other. In this paper, we propose Event Chain Retrieval-Augmented Generation (EC-RAG), a training-free framework that organizes video content into an explicit event chain before question answering. Instead of retrieving isolated frames or text segments, EC-RAG first partitions the video into semantically coherent segments, represents each segment using multi-modal signals, and then links them into a structured chain that preserves temporal order and captures inter-event relationships. Given a query, the system identifies relevant events within this chain and gathers supporting evidence from the associated modalities. Our approach offers several practical advantages: (i) event-level abstraction that better reflects how video content is naturally structured, enabling more reliable localization compared to frame-level retrieval; (ii) structured multi-modal fusion that aggregates speech, text, and visual cues at the event level, allowing complementary information to be more effectively utilized during reasoning; and (iii) plug-and-play compatibility with existing LVLM backbones, requiring no additional training or reliance on proprietary models. Experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench show that this event-centric design consistently outperforms frame-level retrieval baselines, highlighting the importance of modeling temporal structure for long-video understanding.

papers.title: PERSIST: Who-What-When Memory Across Sessions for Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue
papers.summary: Modern voice assistants may be shared by multiple users and should be able to answer questions about earlier conversations such as "When did I originally plan to leave?" or adapt their behavior to individual users based on past interactions. This requires more than retrieving a topically similar passage: the assistant must identify the current speaker, recover the relevant past state, and distinguish it from later revisions. We present PERSIST, a persistent memory system for multi-session, multi-speaker spoken dialogue that explicitly models Who, What, and When. PERSIST structures cross-session histories into readable event records and retrieves them with a 3W joint scoring mechanism that combines semantic content, acoustic speaker identity, and temporal state. For real-time full-duplex interaction, PERSIST further reuses intermediate representations from the dialogue backbone, avoiding query-audio re-encoding and reducing retrieval latency from 578.42 ms to 7.03 ms. We also introduce SpokenTrace, a diagnostic benchmark that factorizes evaluation along memory tasks and speaker-query types, exposing failures in recall, speaker attribution, and temporal-state tracking. On SpokenTrace, PERSIST achieves 85.08% end-to-end task accuracy and improves all-support EM@3 from 49.01% with BGE-large to 82.10%.

papers.title: Logbook: Extremely Long-form Audio Event Understanding
papers.summary: Audio benchmarks are built around short, pre-segmented clips, limiting model design to brief inputs or fixed vocabularies. To close this gap, we introduce Logbook, a benchmark for hour-scale audio understanding, with recordings ranging from ten minutes to six days. Given a continuous audio recording and an event label vocabulary, a system must predict a gap-free segmentation with an event label and a description per segment. We compare 52 systems, end-to-end and cascaded, and ablate fine-tuning, context length, and reasoning budget. We find the task tractable, though the best systems remain below the human reference. Also, over-segmentation is pervasive, and fine-tuning partially mitigates it. Finally, end-to-end are often better than cascaded systems, but degrades with longer context.

papers.title: Harmful Content Generation in Text-to-Image Models: Capabilities and Moderation Limitations
papers.summary: Text-to-image generative models can produce highly realistic imagery but also raise concerns about harmful misuse. While safety mechanisms exist, systematic evaluations of their effectiveness against realistic attacks remain limited. We present a systematic evaluation of harmful content generation across five open text-to-image models using an automated pipeline that transforms legitimate news captions into unsafe prompts targeting sexually explicit content, violence/gore, harmful stereotypes, self-harm, and hate speech. We evaluate both standard models with built-in safety mechanisms and community fine-tuned variants that bypass content restrictions. A human evaluation of 1,500 generated images shows high harmful-content generation rates: 89.2% for gore-related prompts, 47.6% for sexually explicit content, 43.6% for harmful stereotypes, 46.0% for hate speech, and 34.5% for self-harm, predominantly through graphic violence. Models show substantial capability for generating violent and stereotypical content, while community fine-tuned variants are particularly vulnerable to sexually explicit prompts. Generation quality is largely preserved under harmful prompting, producing imagery of sufficient fidelity to pose risks for disinformation and abuse; FLUX.1-dev produces clearly realistic harmful images in 30.9% of cases. We further evaluate automated moderation systems and find substantial detection gaps that allow unsafe images to evade filtering. Finally, we assess synthetic image detectors and show that models trained only on benign datasets perform worse on explicit content, while more diverse training data improves detection, highlighting semantic distribution gaps in current approaches. These findings expose limitations in current generation safeguards, moderation systems, and synthetic image detection, highlighting the need for stronger defenses against misuse at scale.

papers.title: When Layer Selection Misleads Speech Depression Detection
papers.summary: Pretrained speech representations are increasingly used for depression detection, but selecting the best encoder layer on the same data used for evaluation biases reported performance. On DAIC-WOZ, with repeated nested cross-validation across five deep encoder families, naive best-of-25-layer probing inflates AUC by up to $0.09$. On shuffled labels over the \emph{real} latent representations, naive best-of-25 still reaches AUC $0.59$ versus $0.50$ under nested selection, and this bias grows with the number of probed layers and with smaller samples, isolating selection, not signal, as the cause. The effect replicates on a second clinical corpus and language (Androids, Italian). Under leakage-free selection, a fair comparison across representation families identifies a compact, task-aligned affect--prosody model as competitive with substantially more complex SSL, deep-learning, audio-LLM, and codec-based approaches, while using $\sim\!10^{3}\times$ fewer trainable downstream parameters. Extending the analysis to individual PHQ-8 symptoms shows that the same selection bias persists at this finer-grained level. We argue nested model-selection protocols should be standard when probing encoder layer representations on small clinical speech datasets.

papers.title: Revisiting Frame-Wise Saliency for Audio Moment Retrieval
papers.summary: This paper revisits frame-wise saliency for audio moment retrieval (AMR). We show that the frame-wise saliency sequence, conventionally used only as an auxiliary output in DETR-based AMR models, can itself serve as an effective source of moment predictions. We convert the saliency sequence into ranked moments using a simple SED-inspired segmentation rule with no learned parameters, enabling moment retrieval directly from frame-wise temporal information. On the CASTELLA dataset, saliency-based prediction consistently outperforms decoder-based prediction from the same model across all 18 runs of QD-DETR and CG-DETR. For QD-DETR, simply replacing the inference output improves R1@0.7 from 21.0 to 36.1. The advantage remains 7-15 points when the two outputs are evaluated at their independently selected best epochs. The same tendency extends to TaskWeave and UVCOM, whereas TR-DETR shows the opposite behavior, suggesting that how saliency construction may matter. The performance gap is especially pronounced for short moments: for queries whose annotated moments average at most 2 s, R1@0.7 improves from 6.3 to 27.8 with QD-DETR. Decoder supervision nevertheless benefits saliency-based prediction, indicating that its role during training differs from the utility of its inference output.

papers.title: SEA-LM: Egocentric Spatial Audio Understanding for Wearable Microphone Arrays
papers.summary: Embodied, ego-centric intelligence fundamentally requires the ability to comprehend spatial audio within complex environments. While large audio-language models excel at mono-channel reasoning, they lack spatial awareness, discarding critical spatial cues that enable sound localization and that can improve the disentanglement of overlapping sound sources. To address this, we present SEA-LM, a Spatial Audio Understanding model. First, we introduce FOACODER, a layout-flexible spatial audio encoder trained on source localization and ego-centric voice activity detection objectives to encode First Order Ambisonics derived from variable-count, variable-position smart-glasses arrays via beamforming. We train a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) to understand these spatial audio embeddings through a two-stage curriculum spanning six tasks, including sound localization and spatially selective transcription in settings with multiple speakers and overlapping sounds. To prevent the transcription outputs from dominating the next token prediction loss and overwhelming the direction predictions, we introduce a Spatio-temporal Weighted Cross-Entropy Loss. On our evaluation set, SEA-LM achieves lower azimuth and elevation MAE, higher temporal IoU, lower external-source hallucination and missing-source rates, and lower WER on most transcription tasks than compared baselines, while remaining robust across 1,211 smart-glasses array configurations with 4 to 9 microphones.

papers.title: Hallucination Reduction for LLM-Based Audio Understanding via Multimodal Direct Preference Optimization
papers.summary: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) are prone to hallucinating and over-relying on text priors when simultaneously presented with audio and text inputs. To mitigate these hallucinations, we propose utilizing the multimodal Direct Preference Optimization (mDPO) objective, which forces the model to ground its generation in the acoustic input by contrasting intact and distorted audio counterparts. We extend this preference learning framework to the audio domain by applying a variety of acoustic perturbations. Evaluating the Qwen2-Audio backbone across the DCASE 2025 Challenge and AH Existence datasets, we demonstrate that extending mDPO to LALMs significantly enhances temporal reasoning in the complex DCASE dataset, and improves performance on basic existence verification in the AH benchmark. We identify temporal reversal, frequency masking, and random noise as the most effective perturbations. Ultimately, our approach achieves an absolute accuracy improvement of 14.0% on the DCASE 2025 dataset and 27.4% on AH Existence.

papers.title: Indic-CLAP: Text--Audio Understanding in Indic Languages via Cross-Lingual Distillation
papers.summary: Contrastive Language--Audio Pretraining (CLAP) learns a joint text--audio representation space, which enables zero-shot audio understanding from natural-language descriptions. However, its English-only text encoder restricts CLAP to tasks and datasets expressed in English. We present Indic-CLAP, a multilingual text--audio model that extends CLAP to nine Indic languages spoken by over a billion people. Exploiting CLAP's dual-encoder structure, we propose to train only an Indic text encoder by distillation while keeping the audio encoder frozen, using machine-translated AudioCaps captions. We compare distillation from CLAP's text encoder, audio encoder, and a novel hybrid objective combining both. Our evaluation shows that the Indic-CLAP encoder inherits the cross-modal alignment from the CLAP teacher, as evidenced by the performance on cross-modal retrieval and zero-shot classification tasks. Further, we study the cross-modal alignment using modality gap analysis, which explains the performance trends.

papers.title: Collapse, Not Invariance: Diagnosing Auxiliary Objectives in Speech Anti-Spoofing
papers.summary: Speech anti-spoofing countermeasures degrade when the generator, codec or channel changes, and a common remedy is an auxiliary objective that shapes the embedding space; whether it does is invisible to EER, a pure ranking metric. We compare seven such objectives with cross-entropy over 113 runs on five corpora, AASIST3 at three seeds plus four pre-trained detectors, and measure the embedding space of the 24 AASIST3 runs directly. Raw augmentation displacement makes cosine consistency look effective, but the gain is a smaller space, not a more stable one: normalised by the spread, no configuration consistently improves on cross-entropy. Every trained space is dominated by the single decision axis expected for two classes, whose training-set structure does not transfer, and four runs collapse to a near-constant output that displacement rewards and EER reports as poor accuracy. No auxiliary objective keeps an advantage over cross-entropy across architectures, corpora and seeds.

papers.title: MGhana-ST: A Low-Resource Speech Translation Dataset for Ghanaian Languages and an Analysis of Multilingual Training Trade-offs
papers.summary: We present MGhana-ST, a speech translation dataset for four low-resource Ghanaian language varieties: Ga, Twi (Akuapem and Asante), Ewe, and Fante. MGhana-ST is an ongoing annotation effort; the experiments here use a fixed subset of about 16.1 hours of paired speech and English translations. The audio is curated from two existing Ghanaian speech resources. Unlike in those resources, the English translations are produced directly from audio by 37 native-speaker annotators and include verbal and non-verbal event annotations. Using Whisper-small, we compare monolingual and multilingual training under severe data scarcity, reporting means over three seeds. Flat multilingual training benefits no variety in this regime. Ga and Twi are unchanged within seed variance (+0.51 and +0.06 BLEU against monolingual standard deviations of 1.63 and 2.20), while Ewe declines by 6.99 BLEU and Fante by 5.11. The degrading varieties are Ewe, which is linguistically distinct and drawn from a different source corpus, and Fante, the least-resourced. Comparing empirical cross-lingual transfer with typology-based similarity, we find that transfer BLEU identifies closely interacting language pairs better than URIEL similarity, though neither predicts which varieties benefit from joint training. We also report a methodological finding. An earlier single-run analysis found positive transfer for three of four varieties; this did not survive replication across seeds. For Ga and Twi, monolingual baselines trained on 1.6 to 6.2 hours of audio have seed standard deviations roughly five and thirty times those of the multilingual models (0.35 and 0.07 BLEU). When the monolingual condition is noisier, a single-run comparison can show apparent transfer of this size from seed variation alone. We release MGhana-ST to support research on African language speech technology and low-resource speech translation.

papers.title: OmniReasoning: Pushing the Limits of Audio-Visual Joint Reasoning
papers.summary: Recent advances have enabled unified omni-modal models in understanding audio, vision, and language. However, existing benchmarks, training data, and learning methods largely treat the modalities independently, leaving the capability of audio-visual joint reasoning poorly evaluated and insufficiently elicited. We address this gap with a benchmark, data engine, and learning method. First, we introduce OmniReasoningBench, a benchmark where both audio and visual evidence are indispensable. It comprises 1,150 multiple-choice and open-ended questions across two tasks, reasoning over video and reasoning beyond video. Second, we develop a data engine OmniQA. It automatically constructs evidence-grounded QA pairs that explicitly necessitate audio-visual joint reasoning, together with time-stamped clue chains that guide the annotation of thinking process. Besides our benchmark, this engine produces training data OmniReasoning-SFT-112K and OmniReasoning-RL-19K. Finally, we propose an on-policy self-distillation method Modality-Factored Self-Distillation (MFSD). It evaluates each sampled response under modality-specific clue contexts, disentangling the contributions of individual clues and their cross-modal interactions for token-level credit assignment. With our training data and learning method, our model OmniReasoning-30B-A3B achieves 50.0% on OmniVideoBench and 42.5% on OmniReasoningBench, improving the base model Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Thinking by 12.8 and 9.3 percentage points, respectively. Moreover, it delivers substantial gains on general and long-video benchmarks, including Video-MME-v2. We hope our work offers a solid step for facilitating future research in omni-modal joint reasoning.

papers.title: AS$^2$D: Accelerating On-Demand Audio Understanding on Mobile Devices
papers.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by using a smaller drafter to propose tokens for batched verification by a larger target. However, conventional speculative decoding couples drafting to the target's evolving verified prefix, serializing drafting and verification. We ask whether this dependency is necessary for source-conditioned generation. Our key observation is that, for audio language models, the input audio and user request can provide useful speculative candidates without following the target's evolving text prefix. We propose AS$^2$D (Audio Speculative Speculative Decoding), which enables target-decoupled drafting: an audio-conditioned drafter follows its own generation history while the target independently verifies and corrects ready candidates. Without usable candidates, the target advances alone. Thus, target feedback determines which candidates are committed but no longer determines when the drafter can make progress, enabling drafting and verification to proceed concurrently while retaining target-side verification and correction. We implement AS$^2$D in MNN for Android and evaluate two target models across four phones, seven datasets, and three tasks covering 12.2 hours of audio. Across four phones, AS$^2$D improves pooled ASR throughput by 42-76% over target-only decoding, while only 5.7% of evaluation windows are slower than target-only, compared with 58.1-63.0% for speculative baselines. For ASR, AS$^2$D reaches 97.33-98.20% of a hindsight per-window oracle's pooled throughput over the evaluated drafter/budget catalog. Native on-demand execution with a 7B target achieves up to 78% higher throughput than target-only. These results show that source-conditioned audio generation can relax the conventional dependence of speculative drafting on the target's evolving output prefix, exposing substantial parallelism for efficient inference.

papers.title: Repetition, Not Length: Isolating the Counting Failure in Neural Text-to-Speech
papers.summary: Text-to-speech models loop, truncate and lose count on text that repeats a phrase many times. We show that repetition itself is what breaks them, not the length that comes with it. Every repeated sentence in our test set is paired with a control of matched sentence and word count in which no word ever repeats back-to-back. Six models from three architectures render the controls almost perfectly and fail the repeated twins: 94.3% against 18.2% exactly right at k >= 6. The gap survives greedy decoding, repetition-penalty sweeps, four independent speech recognisers and 420 analysis specifications without once reversing sign; a held-out fourth architecture lands within a point of its predicted gap, and one of two non-autoregressive baselines shows the same failure. Varying the period of the text shows the failure grows smoothly with periodicity, half of it surviving when no word is adjacent to itself.

papers.title: When Capabilities Fail to Compose: Diagnosing the Compositionality Gap in Large Audio-Language Models
papers.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) perform strongly on individual audio tasks, but whether these capabilities can be reliably composed remains underexplored. We conduct a controlled diagnostic study of capability composition in LALMs, requiring models to integrate audio-attribute recognition, cue-conditioned segment selection, and downstream ASR or question answering. We construct two-utterance inputs with distinct acoustic cues to evaluate composition across environmental sound, gender, and emotion cues, with ASR, Math QA, and Factual QA as downstream tasks. Across four open-source LALMs, compositional QA accuracy decreases in 39 of 40 model-task-cue settings, by an average of 26.7 percentage points. ASR exhibits a similarly consistent degradation, with WER increasing in 39 of 40 settings by an average of 28.5 percentage points, while the magnitude of degradation varies across models, cue types, and cue salience. We further probe these failures through output format, positional preference, and chain-of-thought (CoT) analyses. Our study reveals a systematic gap between possessing individual audio capabilities and reliably composing them.

papers.title: Does a prosody-trained representation help beyond trainable fusion? A parameter-matched study with frozen HuBERT
papers.summary: Explicit prosodic cues may help automatic speech recognition (ASR) of spontaneous speech, but auxiliary representations typically require additional trainable components, making it unclear whether gains come from the auxiliary information or the fusion mechanism. We address this using a frozen HuBERT backbone and a 64-dimensional representation trained to predict log F0, voicing, Delta log F0, log energy, and spectral tilt. We compare a frozen-backbone recognizer (Baseline), trainable fusion with zero auxiliary input (Null), and the same fusion supplied with the learned representation (Learned). Across Buckeye, Switchboard, and AMI IHM, Null reduces WER by 0.71-1.45 points over Baseline, whereas Learned differs from Null by +0.07, -0.09, and +0.00 points, with no significant differences. However, removing or mismatching the representation at inference increases Learned WER. Thus, Learned depends on the representation yet shows no measurable incremental WER benefit over the parameter-matched control.

papers.title: When Semantics Matter: Reliability-Aware Semantic-Rhythm Control for Co-Speech Gesture Generation
papers.summary: Co-speech gesture generation aims to synthesize natural gestures that are both temporally synchronized with speech and semantically consistent with the spoken content. Although recent methods can generate rhythmically plausible motions, they often rely heavily on acoustic prosody while underutilizing textual semantics, especially when semantic annotations are incomplete, noisy, or unavailable. Consequently, the generated gestures may follow speech rhythm while failing to express the intended semantics. To address this problem, we propose a reliability-aware semantic-rhythm control framework for co-speech gesture generation. We first learn a discrete motion prior that represents continuous gestures in a compact and structured motion-code space. We then introduce a dual-branch semantic contribution estimation mechanism consisting of a full multimodal branch and an audio-only branch. Their distributional discrepancy is formulated as conditional information gain to quantify how much textual semantics changes the predicted motion. Based on this estimate, a controllable semantic-rhythm objective selectively strengthens semantic guidance in content-relevant segments while limiting unnecessary semantic intervention in rhythm-dominant segments. Furthermore, we treat background noise as an acoustic reliability condition and introduce noise-conditioned feature modulation together with beneficial latent perturbation to improve generation robustness under realistic acoustic environments. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a favorable balance among semantic expressiveness, rhythmic synchronization, motion diversity, and robustness, enabling reliable and controllable co-speech gesture generation.

papers.title: When Does a Spoken Agent Have Enough Evidence to Act? The PACT-SLM Contract Test
papers.summary: Streaming spoken agents may produce the correct final action after acting too early. Final-turn scores do not reveal whether each observed speech prefix supports an exposed action. We introduce the Partial Speech Action Contract for Turn Taking in Speech Language Models (PACT-SLM), a controlled test that assigns the first valid action time and evaluates both action identity and timing. In the primary test, 80 paired contrast groups from four held-out semantic families yield 1,600 prefix predictions across clean and 15 dB noise renderings. Using source-utterance semantic targets rather than counterbalanced branch codes, WavLM Base Plus reaches 26.03% pooled post-onset semantic-label accuracy (95% group-bootstrap interval [22.14%, 29.68%]), exposes an action on 18.99% of pre-onset prefixes, and predicts 5.94% of complete trajectories exactly. Its pooled label score is at the 96th percentile of 100 within-prefix label permutations, below the 97.5th-percentile reference (26.73%). It exceeds matched text, scalar-acoustic, and shuffled-representation probes in pooled post-onset label accuracy. Elapsed time is more onset-exact (36.25% versus 23.13%) but less accurate about action identity (9.92% versus 26.03%). These results motivate separate measurement of action identity and onset timing in partial-speech evaluations.
